true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The shorter ticker accelerates every cleanup job, not just annotations

Changing this ticker from ten minutes to one minute makes all cleanup jobs run ten times as often, including filesystem scans, dashboard-version deletion, image deletion, and query-history limit enforcement. It also leaves the nine-minute execution timeout unchanged: if a cleanup cycle takes longer than one minute, a tick will already be pending when it finishes, allowing repeated cycles to run without a pause. This unrelated scheduling change can materially increase database and filesystem load. Preserve the existing interval for this annotation-query fix, or isolate and justify a separate scheduling change.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite ID-list construction performs quadratic copying

For SQLite batches larger than 999, each iteration formats a new string containing the entire accumulated ID list. Building a batch of N IDs therefore copies O(N²) bytes. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands, as explicitly supported by the new test, this creates gigabytes of temporary allocations per full batch and can substantially delay cleanup and increase GC pressure. Build the list with strings.Builder or an append-based byte buffer instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Attribute duration and error metrics to the store actually called

The asynchronous DeleteCollection call records its legacy-store duration and failures through recordStorageDuration, so legacy failures are reported as unified-storage failures and unified-storage timings include legacy work. Conversely, the unified Create and Update error paths at lines 45 and 129 call recordLegacyDuration even though legacy storage was never invoked. Correct these store assignments so operators can distinguish primary-storage failures from failed safety copies.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Do not use resource names as the kind metric label

The successful delete duration passes name in the argument position used for options.Kind by the other metric calls. This creates separate metric series for every deleted resource name rather than a bounded set of kinds, causing unbounded Prometheus cardinality and memory growth as resources are deleted. It also makes successful delete metrics inconsistent with failed delete metrics. Pass the resource kind instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Detach background writes from request cancellation

The legacy write's timeout context is derived from the request context. The HTTP server cancels that parent when the request handler returns, so returning the unified-storage result can immediately cancel the background legacy write rather than give it ten seconds to complete. This affects all four asynchronous write methods and can routinely leave legacy storage unchanged after successful requests. Preserve the request's context values while detaching cancellation before applying the background timeout.

Mirror the resolved update rather than replaying UpdatedObjectInfo

The legacy update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of a wrapper containing the object returned by unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can calculate a PATCH or server-side apply result from the old object supplied by the store. Replaying it against legacy storage, which may be stale because mirroring is asynchronous, can produce a different object or fail even though the unified update succeeded. Pass the resolved unified-storage result to the legacy update, as the previous implementation did, rather than independently recomputing the update against legacy state.

Preserve write ordering when mirroring to legacy storage

Each successful write launches an independent goroutine with no ordering between operations on the same resource. A client can successfully create an object and then delete it, while the legacy delete executes before the legacy create finishes; the create then leaves an object in legacy storage that is absent from unified storage. Consecutive updates can likewise overwrite newer data with older data. Background mirroring needs ordered execution or another mechanism that prevents stale operations from being applied.

Use distinct store mocks and wait for background assertions

The tests give legacy and unified storage the same mock.Mock, so expectations for identically named methods cannot distinguish which store was called. For example, the create failure case configures only setupLegacyFn but that expectation also satisfies the unified Create call. The write tests also return without waiting for or asserting the background legacy calls. As a result, they can pass when writes go to the wrong store or legacy mirroring never happens. Use separate mocks and synchronize assertions on completion of the asynchronous writes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Keep index construction serialized for each namespace/resource key

The cache mutex now protects only publication, so GetIndex returns nil while an index is being built. Concurrent searches, or a search racing with the write-event handler, can therefore build separate indexes for the same key. For in-memory indexes, the last publication replaces the other index and can discard updates already applied by the event handler; for file-backed indexes, both builds attempt to create the same directory and one can fail. Use per-key locking or singleflight around the cache recheck, construction, and publication while allowing different keys to build concurrently.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Synchronize TotalDocs with index-cache writes

The new startup log calls TotalDocs after the write-event consumer has been started. TotalDocs iterates the Bleve backend's cache map without taking cacheMu, while that consumer can build and publish an index for a new namespace or one skipped by InitMinCount. This introduces an unsynchronized map read/write and can terminate the process with 'concurrent map iteration and map write' during startup. Protect TotalDocs's cache traversal with the cache read lock.

false_positives.candidate:
Preserve the stopped-service guard when removing lazy initialization

Removing the Init checks from request handlers also removes their shutdown guard: Stop sets initErr to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped', and previously Init returned that error to subsequent requests. Now Create, Update, Delete, and the other handlers continue using the backend after Stop. The SQL backend's Stop only cancels its pollers, so these writes can still succeed without being propagated to watchers or search indexes. Retain a separate lifecycle-state check even though initialization is now eager.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Register cleanup for the actual provider aliases

The new test creates providers named idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-19, but every cleanup callback removes the literal alias "alias". The additional callback at line 425 has the same problem for idp-alias-20. These callbacks therefore do not remove the created providers and can fail with a not-found response during teardown. In particular, the realm-level providers survive organization cleanup and pollute subsequent tests or cause duplicate-alias failures on another run. Register each callback using the alias of the provider it created.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Use stored enabled state when deciding login-cache invalidation

The original model passed here comes from getById(), which wraps organization-linked providers so that isEnabled() returns false while their organization (or the organization feature in the realm) is disabled. However, getForLogin() populates its cached ID set using the delegate's stored enabled state. For example, cache an enabled public organization provider, disable its organization, then change BROKER_PUBLIC to false. Both predicates here return false, so the cached login list is retained. Once the organization is enabled again, that now-private provider is still returned from the cache and displayed by OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean, which only rechecks isEnabled(). Compare the original and updated persisted provider states, rather than organization-aware enabled states, when deciding whether query membership changed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Provide a compatible default for the new provider method

Adding order() as an abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations: their source no longer compiles, and previously compiled implementations can throw AbstractMethodError when the new provider comparator invokes order(). This also prevents selection of a valid built-in provider when an older custom provider is discovered alongside it. A default implementation would allow existing providers to remain loadable while the built-in providers override their priorities.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Generate the appropriate EC curve for each algorithm

Every test generates a key using the JCA provider's default EC curve, which is normally P-256. Selecting SHA384withECDSA or SHA512withECDSA does not change that key's curve, so the ES384 and ES512 tests only pad P-256 signature components to larger output sizes. They never exercise actual P-384 or P-521 signatures, including the long-form DER sequence length needed for P-521. Initialize the key generator with the algorithm's corresponding curve and verify that the reconstructed DER signature validates the original data, rather than only comparing two conversions performed by the same implementation.

Reject ambiguous highest-priority crypto providers

DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so sorting does not resolve a classpath containing more than one of these providers. The first service-loader entry is silently selected instead of the previous initialization failure. In particular, a classpath containing both the default and FIPS providers can select the non-FIPS implementation based on classpath order. Reject ties at the highest priority, or introduce an explicit selection mechanism, so an ambiguous configuration cannot silently use the wrong cryptographic implementation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Handle existing permission servers that lack the Clients resource

A realm initialized with FGAP V2 before this change has only the Users resource and the previous scopes. AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns immediately when the admin-permissions client already exists, so upgrading does not create the new Clients resource or client-only scopes. For such a realm, the fallback here returns null and is passed to findByResource, followed by an unconditional resource.getScopes() call if execution continues. Client permission checks can therefore fail instead of denying access, and the new client-only scopes cannot be used. Reconcile the schema for existing permission servers and guard against a missing fallback resource.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Global view permission bypasses client-specific denials

canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() grants the all-clients view permission, without evaluating permissions for the requested client. Consequently, an administrator granted view on all clients can still read a client whose client-specific view policy explicitly denies access. This defeats the specific-resource precedence implemented by hasPermission(ClientModel, String). Keep the administrative-role shortcut, but evaluate fine-grained view access through the client-specific permission lookup and its all-clients fallback.

This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

View-only group permission authorizes group creation and moves

canManage() accepts either VIEW or MANAGE on the all-groups resource. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() uses requireManage(), which delegates to this method, so an administrator granted only view permission can create top-level groups or move existing subgroups to the top level by supplying their IDs. Return model group IDs rather than authorization resource IDs

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() passes groupResource.getId() to a helper that looks up resources by their model group ID/name, and then adds that authorization resource ID to the returned set. Authorization resources have independently generated IDs; their names hold the actual group IDs. UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource use this set to restrict user searches by group membership, and user counts also consume it. For example, an all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS grant causes the Groups authorization resource's ID to be returned as a group filter, so searches and counts return no members even though direct user access is authorized. Evaluate the correct resource and return actual model group IDs, including handling an all-groups member grant across real groups.

Choice-format branches bypass HTML validation entirely

`, sanitization produces `a`, and both start and end become 1. The subsequent `sanitized.substring(1, 0)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of reporting illegal HTML. Consequently, the authorization-code, refresh, device, and CIBA event assertions accept tokens with incorrect or unknown grants, hiding failures to propagate the grant context. false_positives.candidate:
Exercise single-use consumption in the federated recovery-code test

The new test provider accepts any matching recovery code without removing or marking it used, and getCredentials reconstructs a fresh credential from the unchanged list on every call. Consequently, the same recovery code can authenticate indefinitely, the displayed code number never advances, and the exhaustion/reconfiguration path is never exercised. The added integration test checks only one successful login, so it passes despite violating the single-use recovery-code contract. Remove exhausted credentials from the storage that owns them

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stop and join the reader before asserting its results

Setting deletedAll to true does not wait for the reader's current HTTP request to finish. The assertion can therefore see an empty caughtExceptions list and pass even if that in-flight request subsequently fails with the NPE this test is intended to catch. Also, if any deletion throws, deletedAll is never set and the non-daemon reader continues making requests after the test fails. Retain the reader thread, signal it to stop in a finally block, and wait for it to terminate before checking caughtExceptions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawned workers fail the Process type check and are never killed

Workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, which produces SpawnProcess instances. SpawnProcess is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check is false for production workers. When a worker is declared hung, it is therefore left running while a replacement is started and its reference is overwritten. The old worker can resume flushing the same shards concurrently with its replacement, and repeated hangs leak workers. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or distinguish processes from threads another way before killing them.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: processes created with `multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process` are instances of `SpawnProcess`, which is not a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process`, causing the `isinstance` check to fail and hung processes to not be killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Do not skip cleanup of remaining workers when the join deadline expires

When the shared join deadline expires, this break exits the worker loop without terminating any remaining workers. For example, if the first worker consumes the timeout waiting on Kafka, all subsequent workers are abandoned even if they are also blocked. Setting stopped only takes effect when a worker returns to its main loop, so it does not stop workers stuck in Redis or future.result(). During rebalancing these workers can remain alive after replacement flushers start. Apply the deadline only to waiting, and perform termination cleanup for every worker regardless of whether time remains.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: breaking out of the worker loop when the deadline expires skips the termination cleanup for the remaining flusher processes/workers, leaving them running. Both suggest ensuring termination is performed for all workers even if the deadline has passed.

false_positives.candidate:
Include the organization in the attribute-key cache key

The new React Query key contains only the query options, although the fetch function calls an organization-specific endpoint. When switching between organizations with identical filters—for example, all projects and the same relative date range—both organizations share a cache entry. Cached custom attribute names from the previous organization can therefore appear in the next organization, and concurrent observers can reuse the wrong organization's response. Include the organization slug or endpoint path in the key.

Normalize error and recording timestamps before merging

Error timestamps read from nodestore are Unix seconds, while rrweb recording event timestamps are Unix milliseconds. Comparing these values directly places virtually every error before the first recording event, regardless of when it actually occurred. The generated error messages also retain the seconds value while recording messages use recording timestamps, giving Seer inconsistent timing context. Normalize both sources to the same unit before comparison and message generation, and test with realistic epoch timestamps.

Only fall back when a custom renderer returns undefined

The custom renderer contract says that returning `undefined` requests fallback rendering, but the implementation uses a truthiness check. Valid React nodes such as `0`, an empty string, or `null` are discarded and replaced with the default cell content. This prevents custom renderers from displaying zero directly or intentionally suppressing a cell. Check `cell !== undefined` in both the body and header renderer wrappers.

The replacement strategy consequently submits to already-shutdown queues. Unlike the bounded batching path, this mode has no limit on outstanding work and can exhaust process memory under sustained load. Drain accepted work and commit it before completing graceful shutdown

close() stops the commit thread before shutting down workers, and pool.shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False). During a rebalance this can leave an old worker modifying subscription state after a new partition owner starts processing replayed results, breaking per-subscription ordering. Graceful close/join must drain accepted work, wait for in-flight processing within the requested timeout, and commit the final completed offsets before returning.

The basic setup flow in this file's tests explicitly creates integration metadata without sender. If such an integration remains after its OrganizationIntegration is removed, attempting to attach it again now raises KeyError and returns a server error rather than a controlled installation failure. false_positives.candidate:
Do not bypass installer verification when the integration is missing

If no Integration row exists for the supplied installation_id, this branch completes the installation without comparing the authenticated GitHub user with the installer. This can happen before the installation webhook is processed or when its delivery fails. The subsequent build_integration fetches the installation using app credentials, which does not establish that the OAuth user has access to it. Consequently, a user supplying another installation's ID can still attach it to their Sentry organization. Fail closed until trusted installer information is available, or verify access using the authenticated user's token.

Compare immutable GitHub user IDs instead of logins

Installer identity is checked using the login saved in webhook metadata and the current OAuth user's login. GitHub usernames can change and old usernames can be claimed by another account. A legitimate installer who renames their account will therefore be rejected, while a different account claiming the old username can pass this check for an unlinked installation. Store and compare the immutable GitHub user ID returned by both the webhook sender and the authenticated-user endpoint.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite ID-list construction performs quadratic copying

For SQLite batches larger than 999, each iteration formats a new string containing the entire accumulated ID list. Building a batch of N IDs therefore copies O(N²) bytes. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands, as explicitly supported by the new test, this creates gigabytes of temporary allocations per full batch and can substantially delay cleanup and increase GC pressure. false_positives.candidate:
Detach background writes from request cancellation

The legacy write's timeout context is derived from the request context. The HTTP server cancels that parent when the request handler returns, so returning the unified-storage result can immediately cancel the background legacy write rather than give it ten seconds to complete. This affects all four asynchronous write methods and can routinely leave legacy storage unchanged after successful requests. Preserve the request's context values while detaching cancellation before applying the background timeout.

Preserve write ordering when mirroring to legacy storage

Each successful write launches an independent goroutine with no ordering between operations on the same resource. A client can successfully create an object and then delete it, while the legacy delete executes before the legacy create finishes; the create then leaves an object in legacy storage that is absent from unified storage. Consecutive updates can likewise overwrite newer data with older data. Background mirroring needs ordered execution or another mechanism that prevents stale operations from being applied.

Mirror the resolved update rather than replaying UpdatedObjectInfo

The legacy update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of a wrapper containing the object returned by unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can calculate a PATCH or server-side apply result from the old object supplied by the store. Replaying it against legacy storage, which may be stale because mirroring is asynchronous, can produce a different object or fail even though the unified update succeeded. Pass the resolved unified-storage result to the legacy update, as the previous implementation did, rather than independently recomputing the update against legacy state.

Use distinct store mocks and wait for background assertions

The tests give legacy and unified storage the same mock.Mock, so expectations for identically named methods cannot distinguish which store was called. For example, the create failure case configures only setupLegacyFn but that expectation also satisfies the unified Create call. The write tests also return without waiting for or asserting the background legacy calls. As a result, they can pass when writes go to the wrong store or legacy mirroring never happens. Use separate mocks and synchronize assertions on completion of the asynchronous writes.

Consequently, members beyond the first 50 are inaccessible on public group pages; previously, non-automatic groups displayed their entire membership. Add public pagination alongside the new server-side limit.

Member removal can leave pagination on an empty, unreachable page

findMembers clamps the offset to the member count rather than to the start of the last populated page, and it calculates that clamp using the count from before the request. If an administrator removes the sole member on page two of a 51-member group, the reload requests offset 50 and returns an empty list with total 50. Subsequent membership changes can clamp the offset to the count itself, still returning no members and potentially reporting page one with Previous disabled. Normalize the offset to a valid page boundary after the total changes and refetch when necessary.

Existing membership PATCH requests silently hide groups

The previous update action supported PATCH /admin/groups/:id with changes[add] and changes[delete], and the resources route still accepts PATCH. The replacement action ignores changes and unconditionally sets visible to false when visible is absent. Existing API callers therefore receive a success response without changing membership, while unintentionally making the group invisible. Preserve the PATCH behavior or explicitly reject the obsolete request before modifying the group.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Update match statistics atomically

The match counter is updated with a read-modify-save sequence. If two requests match the same blocked address concurrently, both can read the same match_count and save the same incremented value, losing one match. The timestamp can also move backward when an older request saves last. Use an atomic database update or a row lock so concurrent validation attempts do not corrupt the blocklist statistics.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same problematic code—updating statistics inside the `should_block_email?` method—and both specifically highlight the race conditions that occur when updating these statistics in a concurrent environment. While the golden comment also points out the architectural smell of having side effects in a query method, the candidate focuses deeply on the concurrency bug aspect mentioned in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Normalize email addresses before matching the blocklist

The blocklist lookup uses an exact, case-sensitive database comparison, and neither BlockedEmail nor the new validator normalizes the address. A blocked address such as `block@spamfromhome.org` can therefore register as `block@SpamFromHome.org`, even though email domains are case-insensitive and this is the same mailbox. Normalize both stored blocklist entries and incoming addresses using the application's email normalization rules before comparing them.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the email blocklist lookup (`BlockedEmail`) performs a case-sensitive comparison without normalization, allowing users to bypass the blocklist by altering the casing of the email address.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Preserve right alignment in the legacy flexbox fallback

The panel now relies on `margin-left: auto` to stay at the right edge, but the `flexbox()` mixin also enables the 2009 `-webkit-box` layout for browsers such as Safari 6. That layout does not distribute free space to auto margins, and the previous `float: right` has been removed. In those browsers the navigation panel sits immediately beside the title/topic information instead of at the right edge. Provide equivalent positioning for the legacy box layout, or retain a working non-flex fallback rather than selecting `-webkit-box`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Apply the website visibility restriction to website_name

The new `website_name` attribute is not included in `untrusted_attributes`, so it is serialized even when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` hides a TL0 user's website from anonymous visitors. The template now displays this unrestricted value, exposing the hidden hostname (and path for matching domains) and bypassing the existing profile-field restriction. Also, `include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?`, so ActiveModel::Serializer will not use it as an inclusion predicate. Add `website_name` to the restricted attributes and cover it in the anonymous TL0 serialization test.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the primary bug mentioned in the golden comment: that the `include_website_name` method is missing the trailing `?` suffix, preventing ActiveModel::Serializer from using it as an inclusion predicate. While the candidate does not mention the secondary string concatenation style issue and adds context about `untrusted_attributes`, it directly hits the core functional bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Imported feed HTML bypasses sanitization

Feed content is passed through Nokogiri fragment parsing and stored as a raw-HTML post, whose cooking method returns the input unchanged. Fragment parsing does not remove scripts, event-handler attributes, or dangerous link schemes. Consequently, active HTML supplied by a feed executes on the forum's origin when the post is rendered, including through the embed template's `raw post.cooked`. Sanitize the imported HTML before storing/rendering it, and escape the URL interpolated into the attribution link.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment identifies two specific issues in TopicEmbed.import: a NoMethodError when contents is nil, and an XSS vulnerability from unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML. While the candidate issue primarily focuses on feed content sanitization, it explicitly identifies the exact same XSS issue at the end: 'escape the URL interpolated into the attribution link.' Therefore, it partially matches the golden comment by catching the XSS vulnerability.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid ERB conditional prevents rendering existing discussions

The conditional ends with `end if`, but the trailing `if` has no condition. ERB generates invalid Ruby for this template, so requests for an embed whose topic already exists fail with a template syntax error instead of displaying the discussion. Close the conditional with just `end`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same syntax error in the ERB template: closing a conditional block with `end if` instead of `end`, which generates invalid Ruby and causes a rendering error.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feeds without a content field abort polling

The poller unconditionally calls `scrub` on `i.content`. Ordinary RSS feeds commonly provide article text in `description` or `content:encoded` rather than `content`, and Atom feeds can provide only a summary. A missing content value therefore raises instead of importing the entry, aborting the entire poll and preventing subsequent entries from being processed. Select the supported content fields with a fallback and handle entries with no body.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug: calling `scrub` directly on `i.content` without checking for nil will raise an exception when an RSS feed lacks the `content` field. Both recommend falling back to `description` or other fields to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Remote retrieval follows redirects outside the allowed host

TopicRetriever validates only the host of the initial embed URL, then this `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects without checking their destinations. An allowed-host URL that redirects to another host, including a private-network address, therefore causes the background worker to fetch that destination and potentially publish its contents as a topic. Validate the scheme and destination address for every request and redirect rather than relying solely on the original URL's host.

URL absolutization mishandles relative and protocol-relative links

The converter only handles values beginning with `/` and treats all of them as paths on the article's host. Thus `images/photo.jpg` remains relative and loads from the forum rather than the source article, while `//cdn.example.com/photo.jpg` becomes a path such as `http://source.example.com/cdn.example.com/photo.jpg`. The same problem affects anchor links. Resolve references against the full source URL with URI-aware joining so imported images and links retain their intended destinations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The second downsize definition replaces the existing API

Ruby does not overload methods by argument count: this definition replaces the downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) method immediately above it. Existing calls with width, height, and options now raise ArgumentError; calls with just width and height bind the height to opts and fail when optimize indexes it as a hash. Keep a single method that explicitly supports both calling conventions, or give the dimensions-string variant a different name.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: the `downsize` method is defined twice, and the second definition (accepting a dimensions string) overwrites the first definition (accepting separate width and height parameters), breaking existing calls to the original method.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Keep the configured size limit for attachments

The hard-coded 10 MB limit applies to attachments as well as images, although the new server-side downsizing only handles images. Attachments larger than max_attachment_size_kb now pass client validation and are uploaded before being rejected by the server. Conversely, sites configured to allow attachments larger than 10 MB can no longer upload them through this client. Retain the configured attachment limit and apply any larger pre-downsizing limit only to images.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same underlying issue: replacing the dynamic per-type site setting (`max_${type}_size_kb`) with a hardcoded 10 MB limit causes the client-side validation to diverge from the server-side and per-type configurations (particularly affecting attachments).

false_positives.candidate:
Downsizing multipart GIF uploads discards their animation

The resize operation receives the multipart tempfile path rather than a path carrying the original filename's extension. Such paths normally have no .gif suffix, but OptimizedImage.optimize selects its animation-preserving implementation only when the input path ends in .GIF. Consequently, even with allow_animated_thumbnails enabled, an oversized animated GIF goes through convert with the [0] frame selector. Because the output overwrites the upload itself, the stored original permanently loses every frame except the first. Determine the image format independently of the tempfile suffix and preserve animation when downsizing the original.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Handle users without an existing TopicUser record

TopicUser.find_by can return nil, but the next statement unconditionally calls notification_level on it. Although sending an email creates a record for its intended recipient, the URL contains no recipient identity and acts on current_user: opening a forwarded email, or opening it while signed into another account that has not visited the topic, produces a 500 response. Initialize the missing per-user topic state and apply the unsubscribe through TopicUser.change, which already supports creating records.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug: TopicUser.find_by can return nil if no TopicUser record exists, and calling methods on this nil object will cause a crash/500 error.

false_positives.candidate:
Do not change notification preferences through an unprotected GET

The new GET route immediately saves a notification-level change for the authenticated user, without a confirmation or recipient-specific token. Rails CSRF protection does not protect GET requests, so an attacker can send a logged-in user to a known topic's unsubscribe URL and silently downgrade or mute its notifications. Serve the confirmation page on GET and perform the change through a CSRF-protected request, or require an appropriately scoped signed token.

Record the unsubscribe as an explicit notification preference change

Saving the TopicUser directly bypasses TopicUser.change, which sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed and records notifications_changed_at. For records whose reason is nil, TopicUser.update_last_read can subsequently replace the unsubscribed regular or muted level with tracking once the reading threshold is reached. The unsubscribe therefore does not persist as an explicit user choice. Use the existing notification-change API rather than only assigning notification_level.

Apply the unsubscribe when entering the route client-side

This route only loads the ordinary topic view; it never invokes the unsubscribe action. Notification preferences are changed solely by the initial Rails GET to the unsubscribe URL. When the Ember application transitions to this route client-side, that GET is not made, yet the template tells the user they will stop receiving notifications. Ensure entering the client route performs the unsubscribe through a protected mutation request before displaying the success message.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Explicitly set updatedAt when touching selected calendars

Passing an empty data object to Prisma updateMany does not advance an @updatedAt field: Prisma leaves the timestamp unchanged for an empty update. Consequently, this new call does not record the cache refresh in SelectedCalendar.updatedAt as its comment claims. Pass an explicit updatedAt value if this tracking is needed, or remove the ineffective call.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: passing an empty data object to Prisma's updateMany does not trigger the @updatedAt decorator to update the timestamp, which breaks cache refresh tracking. Both suggest explicitly setting the updatedAt field.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalidate calendar status after deleting the cache

The cache-deletion success handler does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query; it only invokes an optional onSuccess callback. The wrapper passes its optional onChanged prop rather than refetching this query, and the query disables refetching on window focus. With no callback that explicitly refreshes calendar data, successful deletion leaves the old cache timestamp and delete action visible. Invalidate viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars after deletion so the displayed cache status reflects the database.

false_negatives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check membership in any working interval instead of rejecting against each interval

The new working-hours check rejects a slot if any interval on that weekday does not contain its start. For a normal split schedule of 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00, a 10:00 slot is rejected against the afternoon interval and a 15:00 slot is rejected against the morning interval, removing all availability. Conversely, a weekday with no intervals falls through as available, and the end calculation repeats the slot start rather than using slotEndTime. Require the entire slot to fit within at least one working interval; this is especially important for fixed hosts whose availability must constrain candidates generated by other hosts.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact bug mentioned in the golden comment ('the end calculation repeats the slot start rather than using slotEndTime'), along with other related logic issues in the same working-hours check.

false_positives.candidate:
Date overrides bypass calendar and booking conflicts

When an override exists for the slot's date, checkIfIsAvailable returns true before checking the host's busy intervals. A date override specifies working availability, not permission to ignore existing bookings or calendar events. Consequently, both fixed and round-robin hosts with overrides are treated as available even when they already have a conflicting booking. Continue through the busy-time checks after validating the override.

Preserve the date when shifting override times across midnight

The timezone conversion reduces the shifted override start and end to hour/minute values, discarding any change of date, while activeOverrides is still selected using the unconverted override.start. For example, an Asia/Kolkata override on date D from 01:00–02:00 should appear to a UTC attendee on D−1 from 19:30–20:30. This code selects it for D and adds 19:30–20:30 to D instead, offering availability a day late and omitting the real slots. Convert the complete override interval to actual instants and intersect it with the attendee's day before deriving minute boundaries.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Increment the retry counter atomically

Both failure paths write `reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value read before processing the batch. If cron invocations overlap and both fail to schedule the same reminder with retryCount 0, both write 1, so two failed attempts are recorded as only one and the reminder is retried again instead of being deleted. Use Prisma's atomic increment operation in both paths to avoid losing failed attempts.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency/race condition issue with `reminder.retryCount + 1` in both failure paths and recommend using Prisma's atomic increment operation instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Do not let failure bookkeeping abort the entire reminder batch

The new database update inside the catch block can itself throw, but has no error handling. For example, if a reminder is deleted while the Twilio request is in flight, the update fails because the record no longer exists; a database error in the preceding update can likewise recur here. Previously these per-reminder errors were logged and processing continued. Now the handler exits before processing any remaining reminders, so one failed bookkeeping update prevents unrelated SMS reminders from being scheduled. Handle bookkeeping failures separately so the loop can continue.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

false_positives.candidate:
Removing findMany breaks the existing service API

The service previously exposed findMany(args), which executed a query with authorization and filter conditions applied. This change removes that method and replaces it with getBaseConditions(), which returns SQL rather than query results. Existing consumers of findMany will no longer compile (or will throw at runtime), and consumers of the condition-building methods must also switch from Prisma where inputs to raw SQL. This PR only updates the service and its integration tests; retain a compatible query method or migrate the consumers together with this API change.

Keep the returned base predicate grouped when no filters are present

For team and organization scopes with members, authConditions contains two branches joined by OR. When no service filters are supplied, getBaseConditions returns that expression without enclosing parentheses. Composing it as `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND <date/status condition>` therefore applies the additional condition only to the second branch, because AND binds more tightly than OR. Team bookings in the first branch can then be counted outside the requested date range or status. Return an enclosing parenthesized predicate in this path as well, so the base conditions remain a single expression when used in a larger raw query.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Do not replace an omitted refresh token with a dummy token

This fallback runs even when credential syncing is disabled. Office 365's response schema explicitly allows an omitted `refresh_token`; previously its merge preserved the existing usable refresh token in that case. The helper now inserts the literal `refresh_token`, which overwrites the stored token during the merge. The next refresh sends that dummy value to Microsoft and fails. Preserve the existing refresh token when the provider does not return a replacement.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: when a refresh token is omitted from the OAuth response, the code inserts the hardcoded literal string 'refresh_token', overwriting the valid stored token and causing subsequent refreshes to fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The minimum response schema strips expiry and refresh-token fields

Using a Zod schema's `.toString()` as an object key does not define a wildcard property. These computed keys resolve to literal strings (both normally `[object Object]`), and Zod objects strip unknown properties by default. Consequently, a sync response containing `access_token`, `expires_in`, and `refresh_token` loses the expiry and refresh token during parsing. Zoom then computes an invalid expiry, and Office 365 cannot retain the returned expiry. Define explicit supported fields or use an appropriate catchall/passthrough schema.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug in `minimumTokenResponseSchema`: using `.toString()` on Zod schema objects as computed property keys instead of proper Zod syntax for extra fields. Note that the candidate is actually more technically accurate about the runtime behavior (resolving to `[object Object]` and stripping fields rather than throwing an error), and both clearly point to the same flawed code.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google refresh persists the parse-result wrapper instead of credentials

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a safeParse result shaped as `{ success: true, data: ... }`, unlike the previous `googleCredentialSchema.parse` call, which returned the credential object itself. Saving that result directly as `Credential.key` removes the access token and other required fields from the top level. After the first successful refresh, subsequent GoogleCalendarService instances cannot parse the saved credentials. This also affects installations with credential syncing disabled; persist the parsed `.data` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a Zod `safeParse` result wrapper (`{ success, data }`), and persisting this directly as `key` stores the wrapper instead of the parsed `.data` payload.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync refresh returns a Fetch Response to callers expecting SDK results

The sync branch returns an unparsed Fetch `Response`, while several callers expect the return shape of their original refresh function. Google reads `res.data`, Zoho CRM and Bigin read `tokenInfo.data`, and HubSpot reads `accessToken` and `expiresIn` directly. None of those properties exist on a Fetch Response. Enabling syncing therefore causes those integrations to throw or use undefined tokens even when the endpoint returns valid JSON. Normalize the sync response and adapt each caller to a defined return contract.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: when credential syncing is enabled, the refresh helper returns a Fetch Response object instead of the integration-specific token shapes (like `res.data` for Google or `accessToken` for HubSpot) that callers expect, leading to runtime errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync refresh returns a Fetch Response to callers expecting SDK results

The sync branch returns an unparsed Fetch `Response`, while several callers expect the return shape of their original refresh function. Google reads `res.data`, Zoho CRM and Bigin read `tokenInfo.data`, and HubSpot reads `accessToken` and `expiresIn` directly. None of those properties exist on a Fetch Response. Enabling syncing therefore causes those integrations to throw or use undefined tokens even when the endpoint returns valid JSON. Normalize the sync response and adapt each caller to a defined return contract.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: the sync refresh path returns an unparsed Fetch Response object, whereas the callers (like Google reading `res.data`) expect a parsed object with specific properties, leading to undefined values and runtime errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Pass the Bigin credential owner's user ID, not the credential ID

The third argument to `refreshOAuthTokens` is a Cal.com user ID and is sent to the parent application as `calcomUserId`. This caller passes `credentialId`, which identifies a credential row instead. Those IDs are independent, so the endpoint either cannot find the owner or returns tokens for a different user whose user ID happens to match. Carry `credential.userId` into this method and pass that value.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `refreshOAuthTokens` is being passed `credentialId` instead of the user ID (`userId`/`credential.userId`), which causes incorrect user lookups during token refresh.

false_positives.candidate:
Import Prisma before updating Salesforce credentials

The new code calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file does not import or declare `prisma`. This fails TypeScript checking and, if executed without checking, throws a ReferenceError after the token request succeeds. Import the Prisma client so Salesforce client initialization can complete.

Route Salesforce refreshes through the configured sync endpoint

Salesforce unconditionally refreshes directly against Salesforce instead of using `refreshOAuthTokens`. When syncing is enabled, its parser nevertheless switches to the shared-response schema. Thus Salesforce never asks the configured parent application for refreshed credentials and continues independently refreshing its tokens, contrary to the source-of-truth behavior implemented for the other integrations. Apply the same endpoint routing here before selecting the shared-response parser.

Use the actual Zoom app slug in sync requests

The refresh request sends `appSlug: "zoomvideo"`, but Zoom credentials are installed with `appId: "zoom"` and the webhook identifies apps by their database slug. A parent store using that same slug contract cannot match this refresh to the Zoom credentials it synced. Pass `"zoom"` rather than the integration directory name.

Make first-time credential synchronization atomic

The existence check and credential creation are separate operations, and user/app credentials are not unique. Two concurrent deliveries for a user's first sync can both find no credential and both create one. Future deliveries update only the arbitrary row returned by `findFirst`, leaving another credential stale and available to integration consumers. Serialize this operation or introduce an appropriate unique identity and atomic upsert so concurrent webhook deliveries cannot create duplicates.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Await reminder cancellation work before returning the response

The reminder cancellation helpers are invoked in nested forEach callbacks without awaiting their promises or including them in prismaPromises. Unlike the previous implementation, there is now no awaited database operation that deletes unscheduled reminders or durably marks scheduled emails cancelled. The request can therefore return while these essential writes and SMS cancellations are still running; in a serverless deployment they can be suspended when the response completes, leaving reminders active for a successfully cancelled booking. Collect and await these promises before completing the cancellation request.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug: asynchronous reminder cancellation functions (for email and SMS) are called inside `forEach` loops without being awaited, which can result in reminders remaining active instead of being reliably cancelled.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancel imminent reminders immediately instead of waiting for cron

Scheduled emails are now only marked cancelled, even when their send time is before the next 15-minute cron run. For example, cancelling a booking two minutes before its reminder is due leaves the email scheduled in SendGrid until after it has been sent; the cron then deletes the expired database row before attempting cancellation. Reminders near their send time need an immediate cancellation path rather than unconditional deferral.

Rescheduling bypasses the deferred cancellation mechanism

Rescheduling passes immediateDelete=true for every scheduled email, so cancellations for reminders days in the future still occupy SendGrid's limited pending-cancellation slots until their scheduled dates. This recreates the 100-pending-cancellation failure described in the PR. When that immediate request fails, deleteScheduledEmailReminder only logs the error and never sets cancelled=true, so the cron cannot retry it and the old booking's reminder is still sent. Rescheduling needs the same durable, deferred cancellation mechanism as booking cancellation, except where immediate cancellation is necessary.

Persist successful cancellations before processing the next reminder

Database deletions are accumulated as lazy Prisma promises and executed only after every SendGrid cancellation succeeds. If any request in the loop fails, execution jumps to the outer catch, no successful cancellation is removed from the database, and all subsequent reminders are skipped. The next run consequently retries already-cancelled batches as well as the failed batch, which can fail again and block the remaining reminders until they are sent. Handle failures per reminder and persist each successful cancellation independently.

This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

If calendar synchronization throws, the mutation returns an error even though the guests were added, and notification emails are never attempted. true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawned workers fail the Process type check and are never killed

Workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, which produces SpawnProcess instances. SpawnProcess is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check is false for production workers. When a worker is declared hung, it is therefore left running while a replacement is started and its reference is overwritten. The old worker can resume flushing the same shards concurrently with its replacement, and repeated hangs leak workers. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or distinguish processes from threads another way before killing them.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. Workers created via the spawn context are SpawnProcess instances, which are not subclasses of multiprocessing.Process, so the isinstance check fails and hung processes are never killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

Do not skip cleanup of remaining workers when the join deadline expires

When the shared join deadline expires, this break exits the worker loop without terminating any remaining workers. For example, if the first worker consumes the timeout waiting on Kafka, all subsequent workers are abandoned even if they are also blocked. Setting stopped only takes effect when a worker returns to its main loop, so it does not stop workers stuck in Redis or future.result(). During rebalancing these workers can remain alive after replacement flushers start. Apply the deadline only to waiting, and perform termination cleanup for every worker regardless of whether time remains.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem: breaking out of the loop once the deadline passes skips terminating the remaining flusher/worker processes, so they can keep running. Both also propose the same fix, which is to always attempt termination.

false_positives.candidate:
Include the organization in the attribute-key cache key

The new React Query key contains only the query options, although the fetch function calls an organization-specific endpoint. When switching between organizations with identical filters—for example, all projects and the same relative date range—both organizations share a cache entry. Cached custom attribute names from the previous organization can therefore appear in the next organization, and concurrent observers can reuse the wrong organization's response. Normalize error and recording timestamps before merging

Error timestamps read from nodestore are Unix seconds, while rrweb recording event timestamps are Unix milliseconds. The generated error messages also retain the seconds value while recording messages use recording timestamps, giving Seer inconsistent timing context. false_positives.candidate:
Recreate the queue pool when a strategy is recreated

The factory creates one queue pool in its constructor and passes that same pool to every strategy. During a Kafka rebalance, Arroyo closes the old strategy and creates another through create_with_partitions; closing the old strategy shuts down this pool's queues and workers. The replacement strategy consequently submits to already-shutdown queues. Those submissions raise, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches the exceptions and marks the offsets complete, so results received after a rebalance can be committed without being processed. The pool and its offset tracker need a lifecycle tied to the individual strategy rather than being reused after shutdown.

Bound queued work and apply backpressure

Each queue is constructed without a maxsize, and submission always accepts more work without raising MessageRejected. If result processing is slower than Kafka consumption—or one worker is blocked—the consumer continues retaining decoded results, original Kafka messages, and offset-tracking entries indefinitely. Unlike the bounded batching path, this mode has no limit on outstanding work and can exhaust process memory under sustained load. Bound outstanding work and reject submissions until capacity becomes available.

Drain accepted work and commit it before completing graceful shutdown

close() stops the commit thread before shutting down workers, and pool.shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False). Workers therefore exit after their current item rather than draining accepted queued items; completions after the commit thread exits are never committed. In addition, worker.join(timeout=5.0) can return while a result processor is still running, and strategy.join() ignores its supplied timeout and simply calls close() again. During a rebalance this can leave an old worker modifying subscription state after a new partition owner starts processing replayed results, breaking per-subscription ordering. Graceful close/join must drain accepted work, wait for in-flight processing within the requested timeout, and commit the final completed offsets before returning.

Consequently, members beyond the first 50 are inaccessible on public group pages; previously, non-automatic groups displayed their entire membership. Member removal can leave pagination on an empty, unreachable page

If an administrator removes the sole member on page two of a 51-member group, the reload requests offset 50 and returns an empty list with total 50. true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Update match statistics atomically

The match counter is updated with a read-modify-save sequence. If two requests match the same blocked address concurrently, both can read the same match_count and save the same incremented value, losing one match. The timestamp can also move backward when an older request saves last. Use an atomic database update or a row lock so concurrent validation attempts do not corrupt the blocklist statistics.

The candidate covers the race condition from the non-atomic stats update in the same code, but not the side-effect/misleading-name concern. The overlap on the stats-update race in the same method is substantial, so this is a partial but meaningful match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

Normalize email addresses before matching the blocklist

The blocklist lookup uses an exact, case-sensitive database comparison, and neither BlockedEmail nor the new validator normalizes the address. A blocked address such as `block@spamfromhome.org` can therefore register as `block@SpamFromHome.org`, even though email domains are case-insensitive and this is the same mailbox. Normalize both stored blocklist entries and incoming addresses using the application's email normalization rules before comparing them.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the same problem: the blocklist lookup compares emails case-sensitively, so a blocked address can get through by changing letter case.

-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
